latin.2469: XXXI. Caeterum agnoscunt gratiam, quae uno respectu sufficiens tantum est, alio respectu esse efficacem. Nempe quae sufficiens est respectu actus alicujus perfecti, ad quem disponit, & ad quem ordinatur, efficax est respectu actuum imperfectorum, per quos homo ad actum illum perfectum disponi solet. Imo quamvis, ex eorum mente, omnis gratia sufficiens inefficax sit, ad plenum illud opus, ad quod dicitur esse sufficiens; est tamen plenissime & cumulatissime efficax ad actum proximum & immediatum, ad quem a Deo datur & destinatur.
latin.2470: XXXII. Id inter alios docet expresse Didacus Alvarez numero tertio capitis jam citati. Omne, inquit, auxilium sufficiens, comparatione unius actus, semper est efficax respectu alterius, ad quem efficiendum decreto absoluto divinae voluntatis destinatur. Ut, verbi gratia, auxilium sufficiens ad actum fidei, efficaciter producit in homine pias cogitationes, & notitias credendorum, vel pia desideria habendi fidem, & alios hujusmodi actus imperfectos, qui regulariter loquendo antecedunt assensum fidei. Similiter auxilium sufficiens ad actum contritionis producit efficaciter in homine considerationem poenarum inferni, vel attritionem, aut alios hujusmodi actus imperfectos qui regulariter perfectam contritionem antecedunt.
latin.2471: XXXIII. Porro cum gratia quae sufficiens vocatur, sic dicatur relate ad diversa opera, ad quae hominem disponit, & respectu quorum illi posse donat, prout de variis operibus agitur: ita gratia illa sufficiens, in variis constituenda est. Nec enim eadem gratia hominem ad omnia sufficientem reddit. Sic in homine justo, gratia sufficiens ad opera verae pietatis, & quae vita aeterna digna sint, consistit tum in ipsa gratia habituali, & spiritus sancti donis, quibus jam praeditus est, tum in variis illustrationibus & illuminationibus, quibus ad haec & illa opera invitatur & sollicitatur. In homine fideli, & nondum justificato, fides cum ejusmodi spiritus sancti motibus, auxilium sufficiens est ad orandum & petendum ac impetrandum a Deo gratiam justificantem, & donum spiritus sancti. Et in eo qui nondum fidelis est, gratia sufficiens ad fidei actum sunt, ut jam dixit Alvarez, notitia credendorum, piae cogitationes, & pia desideria habendi fidem, & quae sunt ejusmodi.
latin.2472: XXXIV. Sed quicquid sit, Doctor ille vult nullam gratiam sufficientem esse ad ullum bonum opus, & piam operationem, nisi eam quae non tantum intellectum intus illustrat, sed voluntatem etiam quodammodo movet & afficit. Gratia excitans, inquit, qua illustratur, vel movetur solus intellectus, non est idem quod gratia sufficiens, simpliciter loquendo; sed solum secundum quid: quia non solum intellectus, sed etiam voluntas indiget motione divina, & praeveniente gratia, qua potens reddatur ad opera pietatis exercenda, eo quod voluntas magis corrupta est per peccatum quam intellectus.
latin.2473: XXXV. Hoc autem inde probat quod, Ad salutem non solum est necessarium, ut intellectus cognoscat quid faciendum sit, quidve fugiendum; sed etiam oportet quod voluntas velit bonum amplecti, & malum fugere, ac Deum super omnia diligere: sed per gratiam excitantem in solo intellectu receptam, non potest voluntas aliquid velle, quod sit ad salutem conducens, nec Deum super omnia diligere: Quia gratia existens in intellectu, extrinseca est voluntati; ac per consequens, non tribuit illi sufficiens principium, quo possit opera pietatis exercere. Unde concludit, solam gratiam in intellectu receptam, non esse gratiam sufficientem ad salutem. Epit. de Auxiliis lib. 3. cap. 16.
latin.2474: XXXVI. Auxilium autem gratiae efficacis proprium recentiores illi Thomistae constituunt in gratuita & benigna Dei operatione, quae proprie in libero hominis arbitrio operatur ipsam conversionem, seu alium quemcunque actum verae pietatis. Videlicet ipsum voluntatis motum efficienter attingendo, hoc est, voluntatem ipsam applicando & determinando ad volendum & eligendum. Quae operatio Physica vocatur, id est, proprie dicta. Qualis nimirum agnoscitur in Deo ad alios quoscunque effectus ab ipso procedentes. Quoniam vero fieri nequit ut Deus voluntatem determinet, & non ipsa determinetur, agatque id ad quod tanquam causa secunda applicatur a Deo; sequitur, fieri non posse ut gratia ista non habeat suum effectum. Unde hac ratione, juxta hanc sententiam, efficax dicitur Gratia Dei efficacitate non morali, sed physica & propriissime dicta. Quae verba sunt Estii in 2. sentent. dist. 28. paragr. 2.
latin.2475: XXXVII. Inde est quod gratiam illam dicunt esse efficacem per se, id est, talem quae vi sua movet & determinat liberum arbitrium: idque, ut ipsi loquuntur, infallibiliter, insuperabiliter, indeclinabiliter: quoniam fieri non potest ut voluntas humana illam effectu suo frustretur, obstetque ne praestet illud ad quod proprie a Deo donatur; propterea quod haec divina gratia omnem hominis resistentiam vincit, & vis ejus in eo consistit, ut homo fiat ex nolente volens.
latin.2476: XXXVIII. Quapropter etiam dicunt efficaciam gratiae istius esse absolutam, respectu bonae actionis, nec pendere a consensu liberi arbitrii: quia ut bona actio sequatur, non expectat liberi arbitrii consensum, sed eum potenter efficit; utpote quae liberum sibi subjicit arbitrium, nequaquam vero ejus potestati subjicitur.
latin.2477: XXXIX. Nec tamen putant per istam gratiae efficaciam voluntatis humanae libertatem ulla ex parte, vel tolli vel minui; & propterea minus esse liberas bonas hominis operationes, quae a gratia ista ut a causa sua pendent. Idque quia Deus per gratiam suam, non simpliciter facit ut faciamus opera bona, & ejus voluntati conformia, verum etiam facit ut ea faciamus, secundum modum humanae naturae convenientem, adeoque libere. Siquidem efficax illa gratiae divinae motio id praestat in nobis, ut ex praevio judicio intellectus practici bonum eligamus, & quidem ita, ut ex diverso ejusdem intellectus judicio possemus malum eligere: quod ad plenam rationem libertatis sufficit. Nam quamvis gratia certo & infallibiliter praestet, ut in bonum hoc aut illud voluntate nostra feramur, praevio mentis practicae judicio: non tamen obstat quominus intellectus ejus ductum sequens retineat potestatem aliter judicandi, & voluntas potestatem aliter eligendi, qua in re ratio libertatis sita est. Nempe omnino liber est, qui ex se ad agendum, aut non agendum ita indifferens est, ut dum agit potestatem habeat non agendi, aut aliter agendi.
latin.2478: XL. Quamvis enim gratia efficaciter operetur, ut liberum arbitrium moventi gratiae consentiat, & ductum illius sequatur, non tamen tollit ab eo dissentiendi potestatem. Praestat quidem Christi auxilium efficax ut hominis voluntas, & semper & certissime amplectatur bonum illud ad quod movetur; sed non impedit, quominus dum gratia illam movet, potentiam semper habeat non faciendi tale bonum, imo etiam malum oppositum faciendi. Nempe, ex Doctorum istorum sententia, actualis creatae voluntatis dissensus, cum actuali motione gratiae efficacis consistere non potest; sed tamen cum eadem motione optime consistit potentia dissentiendi. Et hoc est quod dicit Alvarez liberum arbitrium motum a Deo auxilio efficaci, non posse illi dissentire in sensu composito, sed in sensu diviso.
latin.2479: XLI. Porro Jansenius & qui eum sequuntur, eadem cum Thomistis recentioribus docent, circa modum quo Christi gratia medicinalis & efficax in voluntates humanas operatur, easque ad agendum movet. Nempe cum illis volunt efficaciam gratiae illius esse absolutam, nec a consensu liberi arbitrii pendere, & eum expectare, ut effectum suum sortiatur. Illam esse cordis humani victricem, & talem cui nemo valeat resistere. Eam inseparabiliter adjunctum habere effectum ob quem a Deo praebetur: Et a nullo corde quantumvis duro respui, quia ideo praestatur ut ipsa cordis durities auferatur. Illam non relinquere voluntatem in aequilibrio, sed potentissime secum abripere: adeoque illam voluntati humanae inseparabiliter & indeclinabiliter dominari. Quibus similia multa legere est apud dictum Jansenium totis octo libris de gratia Christi salvatoris, praecipue libro tertio.
latin.2480: XLII. Imo idem ille cum Thomistis asserit, huic Christi adjutorio vere competere officium voluntatem physice praedeterminandi. Quippe tale illud esse ut voluntatem ad actum pertrahat, non si voluerit, sed ei efficacissime praebendo ut velit. Quoniam non expectat ut voluntas secum influat, sed facit secum influere voluntatem, applicans eam ad volendum agendumque, quicquid per eam Deus volendum agendumque constituerit. Cum enim per terrenas cupiditates, ut ait, voluntas ad non volendum, imo ad repugnandum determinata sit; tollit istam depressionem, atque determinationem in contrarium, & reflectit eam in bonum, non solum si libero arbitrio hoc videatur, & velit; sed ineffabili sua luce atque suavitate, faciendo ut ei sic videatur, & velit. Sic Deus, juxta ipsum, ex nolentibus & repugnantibus volentes & consentientes facit; voluntatem, scilicet, inclinando, applicando, determinando, & quia praevenit ipsam voluntatis determinationem, etiam praedeterminando; non solum moraliter, sed vera, reali & physica determinatione. Quoniam moralis praedeterminatio illa dicitur quae tantum se habet ex parte objecti, & per modum allicientis, blandientis, rogantis, consulentis &c. sive extrinsecus, sive intrinsecus; sed haec se habet in ipsa potentia voluntatis, quam proprie suae suavitatis magnitudine ad volendum applicat, & applicando determinat, utpote causans in ea hoc ipsum ut se determinet, ideoque praedeterminat. De gratia Christi salvatoris lib. 8. cap. 3.
latin.2481: XLIII. Eadem quoque cum Thomistis ratione, Episcopus iste, & qui doctrinae illius adhaerent, jam descriptam gratiae Christi efficaciam, cum Arbitrii humani, in hoc statu, libertate conciliari posse docent. Nimirum quia illa Christi gratia quae voluntatem ad agendum determinat, ab ea minime tollit potestatem aliter agendi, etiamsi infallibiliter efficiat ut agat. Agens autem illud liberum censeri debet, quod sic agit, ut habeat potestatem non agendi, aut aliter agendi. Neque ad libertatem necesse est, ut cum omnibus ad agendum requisitis stet simul ut non agat voluntas; sed solum ut possit non agere. Itaque, secundum illorum hypotheses, posita gratiae divinae motione, necesse est quidem in sensu composito animum illam sequi, nec potest voluntas Deo moventi resistere, & dissentire ab eo quod per eam vult operari Deus; adeoque vis divinae gratiae eo respectu recte dicitur indeclinabilis & insuperabilis: sed tamen in sensu diviso verum est, voluntatem, etiam quum gratia illam movet, posse Deo resistere, gratiae dissentire; & alio quam quo Deus illam ducit declinare: quia dum gratiae consentit, non propterea amittit potentiam dissentiendi, & dum Deo moventi cedit, potentiam resistendi, ac dum sequitur Dei ductum, potentiam divertendi quo trahit concupiscentia. Ut videre est apud Jansenium de gratia Christi salvatoris lib. 8. cap. 4. Sicut ergo, inquit, in sensu composito verae sunt ejusmodi Phrases, quibus voluntas acta per divinam gratiam, dicitur non posse resistere Deo, non posse dissentire ab eo quod per eam vult operari Deus, non posse declinare, non posse superare: ita e contrario in sensu diviso verae sunt, quibus dicitur posse declinare, posse dissentire, posse superare.
latin.2482: XLIV. Quibus similia repetit & inculcat ejusdem libri capite vigesimo. Dicimus, inquit, liberum arbitrium quantumcunque vehementi atque efficaci gratiae delectatione praeventum atque determinatum ad faciendum bonum, adhuc tamen posse bonum non tantum non facere, sed etiam malum. Verum est istud non quidem in sensu composito, ut vulgo dici solet, sed in sensu diviso. Nimirum quia eodem tempore, quo voluntatis arbitrium sub gratiae delectatione efficaciter eam movente positum est, imo quo etiam actum voluntatis bonum facit, est in eadem voluntate potestas illud non faciendi, imo peccandi; non quod cessatio ab actu quem tunc elicit, aut actuale peccatum cum gratiae delectantis influxu consistere possit, (quod sensus compositus postularet) sed quia cessandi & peccandi potestas cum eadem gratia, simul in eodem voluntatis arbitrio conjungi potest. Nam quamvis duo actus contrarii sint oppositi, & in eadem voluntate simul esse non possint: potestates tamen ad opposita non sunt oppositae, nec sibi invicem, nec actibus oppositis, & in eodem simul subjecto, sive agente, sive quiescente commorantur. Sic ergo voluntas quantumcunque gratiae suavitate capiatur, potest non agere id quo rapitur, quia veram non agendi potestatem, etiam sub gratia rapiente retinet: quamvis fieri nequeat ut ipsa non actio, cum gratiae operatione in eadem simul voluntate copuletur. Quod capite sequenti paucioribus complectitur, Potentia quippe, inquit, dissentiendi non repugnat actuali gratiae motioni & consensui; quamvis fieri nequeat ut actualis dissensus, cum actuali Dei motione jungatur.
latin.2483: XLV. Quanquam vero Jansenius, & qui sunt in eadem cum ipso sententia, agnoscant cum gratiae divinae efficacia sic esse conciliandam indifferentiam, seu potestatem illam, ad bonum & ad malum, ad agendum & non agendum, quam non negant in iis omnibus reperiri qui degunt in hoc mortali corpore; & in qua multi ipsam libertatis essentiam constituere videntur: nihilominus pertendunt inde petendam non esse veram genuinamque divinae gratiae cum libera voluntate concordiam. Quoniam Augustinus & primi ejus discipuli concordiam istam aliter instituunt. Nimirum ut gratiam cum libero arbitrio concilient, simpliciter dicunt, eam idcirco non tollere liberum arbitrium, quia facit ut liberum arbitrium non instar lapidis otiosum sit & nihil agat, nec ut invitum cogatur ad bonum, sed ut etiam ipsum velit & agat, liberum enim definiebant quod est in nostra potestate: hoc autem in nostra esse potestate dicebant quod fit quando volumus, seu quod aliquis si vult facit, si non vult non facit. Quibus positis sequitur omnem omnino voluntatem, seu volitionem rationalem liberam esse: quia quemadmodum impossibile est, ut non fiat quando volumus, & fiat quando nolumus, ita consequenter impossibile est, ut non sit in nostra potestate, & hoc ipso libera non sit. Ac proinde cum gratia non aliud praestet quam ut volitionem bonam, ex rationis recto judicio, eliciamus, hoc ipso facit ut libere agamus, nec libertatem nostram destruit sed astruit. Quam rationem conciliandi libertatem humanam cum infallibili gratiae divinae efficacia, omnium optimam & maxime genuinam existimat esse Jansenius de Gratia Christi Salvatoris lib. 8. cap. 19. Idque quoniam, juxta ipsum, essentia libertatis in genere consideratae, minime consistit in indifferentia, qua potest aliquis velle vel non velle, istud velle, vel contrarium: sed in eo potius quod aliquis ad volendum & agendum, non aliqua vi externa, nec bruta necessitate, sed propriae rationis judicio movetur, & eatenus est actus sui Dominus.
latin.2484: XLVI. Caeterum quanquam Jansenius & Thomistae recentiores in eo conveniunt quod gratia Christi, per quam homines convertuntur & bene operantur, sit gratia per se efficax, quae liberum sibi subjicit arbitrium, nequaquam vero libero arbitrio subdita est; & quae, ut effectus illius sequatur, voluntatis humanae consensum non expectat, sed consensum illum infallibiliter & potenter efficit: inter se tamen dissentiunt de gratiae illius natura atque substantia: nec eodem modo explicant qua in re consistat atque posita sit. Utrisque gratiae istius modus operandi idem est, diversa vero illius essentia.
latin.2485: XLVII. Constat quidem inter utrosque gratiam illam, sine qua nullus ad Deum convertitur & bene agit, & quam omnes qui accipiunt, certo & infallibiliter convertuntur & bene agunt, esse auxilium quoddam quod voluntatem ipsam per se & immediate movet atque afficit, non vero intellectum solum; nec eam in ullo habitu permanenti constituendam esse. Sed quid illa sit, inter hos & illos non omnino convenit: imo nequidem inter ipsos Thomistas.
latin.2486: XLVIII. Licet enim omnes illi efficax istud auxilium nomine praedeterminationis physicae significent, & dicant esse gratuitam & praeviam Dei motionem, quae voluntatem creatam movet & applicat ad bene operandum; nonnulli tamen sunt qui dicunt praemotionem illam Dei qua voluntates humanae ad bene agendum moventur, se habere ad modum qualitatis non permanentis, sed transeuntis cum operatione voluntatis ipsius. Alii vero dicunt motionem actualem qua Deus movet & applicat voluntatem ad operandum, esse realiter ipsam voluntatis operationem, quatenus procedit a Deo, voluntatem ad agendum applicante & praemovente efficaciter. Denique alii pertendunt motionem illam praeviam, nec se habere ad modum qualitatis in voluntate receptae, nec esse idem cum ipsa voluntatis operatione; sed aliquid quod habet esse quoddam incompletum, per modum quo colores sunt in aere, & virtus artis in instrumento artificis, quod proprio & convenienti nomine dici potest motio virtuosa. Ut apud Didacum Alvarez videre est lib. 3. de Auxiliis divinae gratiae disput. 19. ubi postremam hanc sententiam tanquam veram & suam tuetur.
latin.2487: XLIX. Inde vero colligit istud Dei auxilium, voluntatis creatae actioni praevium, produci in illa effective a solo Deo, & nullo modo dependere efficienter ab influxu voluntatis ipsius: adeoque voluntatem in ordine ad illud praevium auxilium Dei se habere passive: quamvis eadem voluntas se habeat active & libere, in ordine ad actum liberum, ad quem praevio illo auxilio movetur. Disputationis modo citatae numero sexto.
latin.2488: L. Porro Doctores illi agnoscunt istam Dei motionem ad omne bonum opus praeviam & necessariam in potestate hominis non esse; quia datur & negatur ex divino beneplacito. Sed nihilominus affirmant in facultate nostrae voluntatis esse seipsam impedire ne habeat motionem illam. Unde colligunt quod, si non operetur actum, qui est in praecepto, imputabitur illi ad culpam, eo quod sua culpa se impedivit, ne daretur illi auxilium efficax, quod necessarium erat, ut actualiter operaretur actum virtutis, qui est in praecepto: sicut si Deus imponeret homini praeceptum volandi, & quantum est ex parte sua, offerret illi alas, & adjutorium necessarium ut volaret; ipse autem sua libertate responderet; Domine nec volo alas accipere nec volare; merito reputaretur reus, & transgressor praecepti, etiamsi non posset absque alis volare, quia sua culpa se impedivit, ne illi donarentur a Deo. Quae sunt verba ejusdem Alvarez libri jamjam citati disputatione decima octava num. 20. Ubi suam doctrinam confirmat Augustini dicto, Ut homines non adjuventur gratia Dei, in ipsis causa est, non in Deo.
latin.2489: LI. Caeterum necessitatem auxilii istius voluntatem efficaciter ad omnem piam operationem praemoventis & praedeterminantis non arcessunt simpliciter ex voluntatis humanae corruptione & infirmitate; sed in genere ex dependentia omnis causae secundae a Prima, sine cujus impulsu & praevia motione, nulla causa est quae quicquam agere possit, juxta ipsorum hypotheses. Ac praeterea ex indifferentia liberae voluntatis, quae non est apta ut aliquid agat, nisi ab agente superiori determinetur.
latin.2490: LII. Quanquam vero istud auxilium efficax in motione quadam voluntatem physice praedeterminante constituant; agnoscunt tamen illud praesupponere motionem moralem, quae fit per objecti propositionem congruam, per quam apparet objectum illud amabile & conveniens voluntati. Nec enim voluntatem posse aliquid appetere, nisi prius per intellectum ei proponatur tanquam conveniens. Ac proinde neminem per auxilium gratiae physice determinari ad bonum prosequendum, quin mens ejus fuerit notitia istius boni illuminata, & voluntas ad illud appetendum invitata, & moraliter inclinata internis spiritus sancti suasionibus & suggestionibus. Verum inde nunquam consequitur, secundum illorum doctrinam, voluntatis consensus, nisi alterum illud auxilium accesserit, quod voluntatem ad consensum illum efficaciter & physice moveat.

sections.title: A grace sufficient for one act is efficacious for another
sections.pass_a: XXXI. However they acknowledge that grace, which in one respect is sufficient only, in another respect is efficacious. Namely that which is sufficient with respect to some perfect act, to which it disposes, and to which it is ordered, is efficacious with respect to imperfect acts, through which man is wont to be disposed to that perfect act. Nay although, in their mind, every sufficient grace is inefficacious, for that full work, for which it is said to be sufficient; yet it is most fully and most abundantly efficacious for the proximate and immediate act, for which it is given and destined by God.
pass_b: Thesis XXXI. They do grant, however, that a grace which in one respect is only sufficient is efficacious in another. A grace that is sufficient for some complete act, toward which it disposes a person and to which it is directed, is efficacious for the incomplete acts by which a person is usually prepared for that complete act.

Indeed, on their view, although every sufficient grace is inefficacious for the full work for which it is called sufficient, it is most fully and most abundantly efficacious for the proximate and immediate act for which God gives and appoints it.

sections.title: Alvarez: sufficient for faith, efficacious for its preparations
sections.pass_a: XXXII. This among others teaches expressly Didacus Alvarez in number third of the chapter already cited. Every, he says, sufficient help, in comparison with one act, is always efficacious with respect to another, for effecting which it is destined by an absolute decree of the divine will. As, for example, sufficient help for the act of faith, efficaciously produces in man pious thoughts, and knowledge of things to be believed, or pious desires of having faith, and other imperfect acts of this kind, which regularly speaking precede the assent of faith. Similarly sufficient help for the act of contrition produces efficaciously in man the consideration of the pains of hell, or attrition, or other imperfect acts of this kind which regularly precede perfect contrition.
pass_b: Thesis XXXII. Diego Alvarez, among others, teaches this expressly in section 3 of the chapter already cited: 'Every aid that is sufficient with respect to one act is always efficacious with respect to another, which an absolute decree of the divine will has appointed it to bring about.

'For example, aid sufficient for the act of faith effectively produces in a person devout thoughts and knowledge of what is to be believed, or devout desires to have faith, and other incomplete acts of this kind which, as a rule, come before the assent of faith. Likewise aid sufficient for the act of contrition effectively produces in a person reflection on the pains of hell, or attrition, or other incomplete acts of this kind which as a rule come before perfect contrition.'

sections.title: Sufficient grace lies in different things for different works
sections.pass_a: XXXIII. Further since the grace which is called sufficient, is so called relatively to diverse works, to which it disposes man, and with respect to which it gives him being able, according as it is a question of various works: so that sufficient grace, is to be placed in various things. For the same grace does not render man sufficient for all things. Thus in a just man, the grace sufficient for works of true piety, and which may be worthy of eternal life, consists both in habitual grace itself, and the gifts of the holy spirit, with which he is already endowed, and in various illustrations and illuminations, by which he is invited and solicited to these and those works. In a faithful man, and not yet justified, faith with such motions of the holy spirit, is sufficient help for praying and asking and obtaining from God justifying grace, and the gift of the holy spirit. And in him who is not yet faithful, grace sufficient for the act of faith are, as Alvarez has already said, knowledge of things to be believed, pious thoughts, and pious desires of having faith, and things which are of that kind.
pass_b: Thesis XXXIII. Since the grace called sufficient is so called in relation to the various works toward which it disposes a person and for which it gives him the ability, according to which work is in question, that sufficient grace must be located in various things. The same grace does not make a person sufficient for everything.

So in a righteous person, the grace sufficient for works of true piety, worthy of eternal life, consists both in habitual grace itself and in the gifts of the Holy Spirit he already possesses, and in the various illuminations and enlightenings by which he is invited and urged toward this or that work. In a believer not yet justified, faith together with such movements of the Holy Spirit is sufficient aid for praying, asking and obtaining from God justifying grace and the gift of the Holy Spirit. And in one who does not yet believe, the grace sufficient for the act of faith consists, as Alvarez has already said, in knowledge of what is to be believed, devout thoughts, devout desires to have faith, and the like.

sections.title: Alvarez: grace in the intellect alone is not simply sufficient
sections.pass_a: XXXIV. But however that may be, that Doctor holds that no grace is sufficient for any good work, and pious operation, except that which not only illumines the intellect within, but also in a certain way moves and affects the will. Rousing grace, he says, by which the intellect alone is illustrated, or moved, is not the same as sufficient grace, simply speaking; but only in a certain respect: because not only the intellect, but also the will needs divine motion, and prevenient grace, by which it may be rendered able to exercise works of piety, because the will is more corrupted by sin than the intellect.
pass_b: Thesis XXXIV. Be that as it may, that doctor holds that no grace is sufficient for any good work or devout action unless it not only enlightens the intellect inwardly but also in some way moves and affects the will.

'Rousing grace,' he says, 'by which only the intellect is enlightened or moved, is not the same as sufficient grace, speaking without qualification, but only in a certain respect. For not only the intellect but the will too needs divine motion and prevenient grace to be made able to perform works of piety, since sin has corrupted the will more than the intellect.'

sections.title: Alvarez's proof: grace in the intellect is external to the will
sections.pass_a: XXXV. But this he proves from this, that, For salvation it is not only necessary, that the intellect know what is to be done, or what to be fled; but also it is needful that the will will to embrace good, and to flee evil, and to love God above all: but through rousing grace received in the intellect alone, the will cannot will anything, which is conducive to salvation, nor love God above all: Because grace existing in the intellect, is extrinsic to the will; and in consequence, does not give it a sufficient principle, by which it can exercise works of piety. Whence he concludes, that grace received in the intellect alone, is not grace sufficient for salvation. Epitome of the Helps book 3. chap. 16.
pass_b: Thesis XXXV. He proves it as follows: 'For salvation it is necessary not only that the intellect know what to do and what to avoid, but also that the will will to embrace good and avoid evil, and to love God above all things. But by rousing grace received in the intellect alone, the will cannot will anything that leads to salvation, nor love God above all things.

'For grace present in the intellect is external to the will, and so it does not give the will a sufficient principle for performing works of piety.' He concludes that grace received only in the intellect is not grace sufficient for salvation. Epitome de auxiliis, book 3, chapter 16.

a sufficient principle

sections.title: The recent Thomists: efficacious grace as God's physical operation (Estius)
sections.pass_a: XXXVI. But the proper help of efficacious grace those recent Thomists place in a gratuitous and kind operation of God, which properly in the free choice of man works conversion itself, or any other act of true piety. Namely by efficiently reaching the very motion of the will, that is, by applying and determining the will itself to will and to choose. Which operation is called Physical, that is, properly so called. Such namely as is acknowledged in God for any other effects proceeding from him. But since it cannot be that God determine the will, and it not be determined, and do that to which as a second cause it is applied by God; it follows, that it cannot be that that grace not have its effect. Whence by this reason, according to this opinion, the Grace of God is called efficacious by an efficacy not moral, but physical and most properly so called. Which are the words of Estius on the 2. of the Sentences dist. 28. paragr. 2.
pass_b: Thesis XXXVI. These recent Thomists locate the aid proper to efficacious grace in a gratuitous and gracious working of God that, properly speaking, produces conversion itself, or any other act of true piety, within a person's free choice. It does so by acting efficiently on the will's very movement, that is, by applying the will itself and determining it to will and to choose. This working is called physical, meaning working in the proper sense, such as is recognized in God with respect to all the other effects that come from him.

Since it is impossible for God to determine the will without its being determined and doing what God applies it to as a secondary cause, it follows that this grace cannot fail to have its effect. 'Hence, on this view, the grace of God is called efficacious with an efficacy not moral but physical, and in the most proper sense.' These are the words of Estius on book 2 of the Sentences, distinction 28, paragraph 2.

lemmas.gloss: by efficiently reaching the very motion of the will
Which operation is called Physical
by an efficacy not moral, but physical

choices.why: Scholastic contrast: a physical motion works on the faculty itself; a moral motion works by attracting and persuading through the object (as XLII and LII explain).

bible_refs: William Estius, Commentaria in quatuor libros Sententiarum, book 2, distinction 28, paragraph 2.
notes: The print numbers this thesis 'XXVI'; corrected to XXXVI (between XXXV and XXXVII).

sections.title: Efficacious of itself: infallibly, insuperably, indeclinably
sections.pass_a: XXXVII. Hence it is that they say that grace is efficacious by itself, that is, such as by its own force moves and determines free choice: and that, as they themselves speak, infallibly, insuperably, indeclinably: since it cannot be that the human will frustrate it of its effect, and hinder that it perform that for which it is properly given by God; because this divine grace overcomes all resistance of man, and its force consists in this, that man becomes from unwilling willing.
pass_b: Thesis XXXVII. That is why they call this grace efficacious of itself, that is, grace that by its own force moves and determines free choice, and does so, in their own words, 'infallibly, insuperably, indeclinably'. For the human will cannot cheat it of its effect or prevent it from accomplishing what God properly gives it for, because this divine grace overcomes all human resistance, and its power consists in making a person willing who was unwilling.

sections.title: Its efficacy is absolute and does not wait for consent
sections.pass_a: XXXVIII. For which reason also they say that the efficacy of that grace is absolute, with respect to the good action, nor depends on the consent of free choice: because that the good action may follow, it does not wait for the consent of free choice, but powerfully effects it; as that which subjects free choice to itself, but in no way is subjected to its power.
pass_b: Thesis XXXVIII. For this reason they also say that this grace's efficacy is absolute with respect to the good action and does not hang on the consent of free choice. For the good action to follow, it does not wait for free choice to consent but brings about that consent by its power, since it brings free choice under itself and is in no way subject to free choice's power.

lemmas.gloss: the efficacy of that grace is absolute

lemmas.latin: non expectat liberi arbitrii consensum, sed eum potenter efficit

sections.title: Freedom kept: the practical judgment could have been otherwise
sections.pass_a: XXXIX. Nor yet do they think that by this efficacy of grace the liberty of the human will is either taken away or diminished in any part; and that therefore the good operations of man are less free, which depend on that grace as on their cause. And that because God through his grace, does not simply make that we do good works, and conformed to his will, but also makes that we do them, according to the mode befitting human nature, and so freely. Since that efficacious motion of divine grace performs this in us, that from a prior judgment of the practical intellect we choose good, and indeed so, that from a different judgment of the same intellect we could choose evil: which suffices for the full notion of liberty. For although grace certainly and infallibly brings it about, that we are borne by our will into this or that good, by a prior practical judgment of the mind: yet it does not hinder that the intellect following its guidance retain the power of judging otherwise, and the will the power of choosing otherwise, in which thing the notion of liberty is situated. Namely he is altogether free, who of himself is so indifferent to acting, or not acting, that while he acts he has the power of not acting, or of acting otherwise.
pass_b: Thesis XXXIX. Yet they do not think that this efficacy of grace removes or lessens the freedom of the human will in any respect, or that a person's good actions, which depend on that grace as their cause, are any less free for it. For through his grace God does not merely cause us to do good works in keeping with his will; he also causes us to do them in the way that suits human nature, and therefore freely.

That efficacious motion of divine grace brings it about in us that we choose the good on the basis of a prior judgment of the practical intellect, and in such a way that, on a different judgment of the same intellect, we could choose evil; and this is enough for freedom in the full sense. Although grace surely and infallibly ensures that our will is carried toward this or that good, with the mind's practical judgment going before, it does not prevent the intellect, while following that guidance, from keeping the power to judge otherwise, nor the will from keeping the power to choose otherwise; and freedom consists in this. A person is wholly free who of himself is so indifferent to acting or not acting that while he acts he has the power not to act or to act otherwise.

lemmas.gloss: from a prior judgment of the practical intellect
suffices for the full notion of liberty

lemmas.latin: ut dum agit potestatem habeat non agendi, aut aliter agendi
lemmas.gloss: that while he acts he has the power of not acting, or of acting otherwise

choices.why: The power to act or not act, or to do this or the contrary; kept as the technical term.

sections.title: The power to dissent: composite and divided sense (Alvarez)
sections.pass_a: XL. For although grace efficaciously works, that free choice consent to the moving grace, and follow its guidance, yet it does not take away from it the power of dissenting. Indeed the efficacious help of Christ brings it about that the will of man, both always and most certainly embraces that good to which it is moved; but it does not hinder, that while grace moves it, it always has the power of not doing such good, nay even of doing the opposite evil. Namely, from the opinion of these Doctors, actual dissent of the created will, cannot consist with the actual motion of efficacious grace; but yet with the same motion the power of dissenting consists very well. And this is what Alvarez says that free choice moved by God with efficacious help, cannot dissent from it in the composite sense, but in the divided sense.
pass_b: Thesis XL. For although grace works effectively so that free choice consents to the grace that moves it and follows its lead, it does not take away its power to dissent. The efficacious aid of Christ does ensure that a person's will always and most surely embraces the good toward which it is moved; but it does not prevent the will, while grace is moving it, from always having the power not to do that good, and even to do the opposite evil.

In these doctors' view, the created will's actual dissent cannot coexist with the actual motion of efficacious grace, but the power to dissent coexists perfectly well with that same motion. And this is what Alvarez says: that free choice moved by God with efficacious aid cannot dissent from it in the composite sense, but can in the divided sense.

sections.title: Jansenius agrees with the Thomists on how efficacious grace works
sections.pass_a: XLI. Further Jansenius and those who follow him, teach the same things with the recent Thomists, concerning the mode in which the medicinal and efficacious grace of Christ works in human wills, and moves them to act. Namely with them they hold the efficacy of that grace to be absolute, nor to depend on the consent of free choice, and wait for it, that it may obtain its effect. That it is victorious over the human heart, and such that no one can resist it. That it has its effect inseparably joined, on account of which it is furnished by God: And by no heart however hard is rejected, because it is furnished for this, that the hardness itself of the heart may be taken away. That it does not leave the will in equilibrium, but most powerfully snatches it away with itself: and so that it rules the human will inseparably and indeclinably. Similar to which things many are to be read in the said Jansenius in the whole eight books on the grace of Christ the saviour, especially in the third book.
pass_b: Thesis XLI. Jansenius and his followers, moreover, teach the same as the recent Thomists about the way in which Christ's healing and efficacious grace works in human wills and moves them to act. With them they hold that the efficacy of this grace is absolute, and that it does not depend on, or wait for, the consent of free choice in order to achieve its effect.

It is, they say, the conqueror of the human heart, and such that no one can resist it. The effect for which God supplies it is inseparably joined to it, and no heart, however hard, rejects it, since it is given precisely to take away the heart's hardness. It does not leave the will evenly balanced but carries it off with the greatest power, and so rules the human will inseparably and indeclinably. Much to the same effect can be read in Jansenius throughout the eight books of De gratia Christi Salvatoris, above all in the third.

choices.why: Jansenius's term for Christ's grace as remedy for the fallen will.

sections.title: Jansenius: grace physically predetermines the will
sections.pass_a: XLII. Nay the same man asserts with the Thomists, that to this help of Christ truly belongs the office of physically predetermining the will. Since it is such that it draws the will to act, not if it wills, but by most efficaciously furnishing to it that it will. Because it does not wait that the will flow in with it, but makes the will flow in with it, applying it to willing and doing, whatever God has determined to be willed and done through it. For since through earthly desires, as he says, the will has been determined to not willing, nay to resisting; it takes away that depression, and determination to the contrary, and bends it back to good, not only if it seems so to free choice, and it wills; but by its ineffable light and sweetness, making that it so seem to it, and it will. Thus God, according to him, from the unwilling and resisting makes willing and consenting; namely, by inclining, applying, determining the will, and because it forestalls the very determination of the will, also by predetermining; not only morally, but by a true, real and physical determination. Since that is called moral predetermination which only holds itself on the part of the object, and by way of one alluring, flattering, asking, counselling etc. whether outwardly, or inwardly; but this holds itself in the very power of the will, which properly by the greatness of its sweetness it applies to willing, and by applying determines, as causing in it this very thing that it determine itself, and therefore predetermines. On the grace of Christ the saviour book 8. chap. 3.
pass_b: Thesis XLII. Indeed Jansenius asserts with the Thomists that the task of physically predetermining the will truly belongs to this aid of Christ. It is such that it draws the will to act, not if the will chooses, but by most effectively granting it to will. It does not wait for the will to act together with it; it makes the will act together with it, applying the will to will and do whatever God has resolved should be willed and done through it.

For since, as he says, the will has been set by earthly desires toward not willing, and even toward resisting, this aid removes that downward pull and that bent in the opposite direction and turns the will back toward the good, not merely if free choice sees fit and wills, but by its own inexpressible light and sweetness, causing it to see fit and to will. So, on his account, God makes willing and consenting people out of unwilling and resisting ones, by inclining, applying and determining the will, and, because he anticipates the will's own determination, by predetermining it too: not only morally but by a true, real and physical determination.

For moral predetermination is the kind that works only from the side of the object, by way of something that allures, coaxes, asks, counsels and so on, whether from outside or within. This predetermination, by contrast, works in the will's power itself, which it properly applies to willing by the greatness of its sweetness, and by applying it determines it, since it causes in the will this very act of determining itself, and therefore predetermines it. De gratia Christi Salvatoris, book 8, chapter 3.

sections.title: Jansenius: freedom saved in the divided sense (book 8, chapter 4)
sections.pass_a: XLIII. By the same reason also with the Thomists, that Bishop, and those who adhere to his doctrine, teach that the efficacy of the grace of Christ already described, can be reconciled with the liberty of human Choice, in this state. Namely because that grace of Christ which determines the will to act, by no means takes from it the power of acting otherwise, even if it infallibly brings it about that it acts. But that agent ought to be judged free, which so acts, that it has the power of not acting, or of acting otherwise. Nor is it necessary for liberty, that with all things requisite for acting it stand at the same time that the will not act; but only that it can not act. Therefore, according to their hypotheses, the motion of divine grace being posited, it is necessary indeed in the composite sense that the soul follow it, nor can the will resist God moving, and dissent from that which God wills to work through it; and so the force of divine grace in that respect is rightly called indeclinable and insuperable: but yet in the divided sense it is true, that the will, even when grace moves it, can resist God, dissent from grace; and turn aside elsewhere than where God leads it: because while it consents to grace, it does not therefore lose the power of dissenting, and while it yields to God moving, the power of resisting, and while it follows the guidance of God, the power of turning aside where concupiscence draws. As is to be seen in Jansenius on the grace of Christ the saviour book 8. chap. 4. As therefore, he says, in the composite sense true are such Phrases, by which the will acted on by divine grace, is said not to be able to resist God, not to be able to dissent from that which God wills to work through it, not to be able to turn aside, not to be able to overcome: so on the contrary in the divided sense those are true, by which it is said to be able to turn aside, to be able to dissent, to be able to overcome.
pass_b: Thesis XLIII. On the same reasoning as the Thomists, that bishop and those who hold to his teaching maintain that the efficacy of Christ's grace just described can be reconciled with the freedom of human choice in this state. The grace of Christ that determines the will to act in no way removes its power to act otherwise, even though it infallibly causes it to act. An agent should be judged free if it acts in such a way that it has the power not to act or to act otherwise. Freedom does not require that the will's not acting be compatible, at the same moment, with everything needed for action being present; it requires only that the will be able not to act.

So on their assumptions, once the motion of divine grace is given, the soul must indeed follow it in the composite sense; the will cannot resist God as he moves it, or dissent from what God wills to accomplish through it, and in that respect the force of divine grace is rightly called indeclinable and insuperable. In the divided sense, however, it is true that the will, even while grace moves it, can resist God, dissent from grace and turn aside elsewhere than God is leading it. For in consenting to grace it does not thereby lose the power to dissent; in yielding to God's motion it does not lose the power to resist; and in following God's lead it does not lose the power to turn aside where concupiscence draws it.

This is set out in Jansenius, De gratia Christi Salvatoris, book 8, chapter 4: 'As in the composite sense those expressions are true which say that the will, acted on by divine grace, cannot resist God, cannot dissent from what God wills to accomplish through it, cannot turn aside, cannot overcome; so, conversely, in the divided sense those are true which say that it can turn aside, can dissent, can overcome.'

sections.title: Jansenius, book 8, chapters 20-21: powers to opposites are not opposed
sections.pass_a: XLIV. Similar to which he repeats and inculcates in the twentieth chapter of the same book. We say, he says, that free choice however vehemently and efficaciously forestalled and determined by the delight of grace to doing good, can nevertheless still not only not do the good, but also do evil. That is true not indeed in the composite sense, as it is commonly wont to be said, but in the divided sense. Namely because at the same time, in which the choice of the will is placed under the delight of grace moving it efficaciously, nay in which it also does the good act of the will, there is in the same will the power of not doing it, nay of sinning; not that cessation from the act which it then elicits, or actual sin can consist with the influx of delighting grace, (which the composite sense would demand) but because the power of ceasing and of sinning can be joined with the same grace, at the same time in the same choice of the will. For although two contrary acts are opposed, and cannot be in the same will at the same time: yet powers to opposites are not opposed, neither to each other, nor to opposite acts, and dwell together at the same time in the same subject, whether acting, or resting. Thus therefore the will however much it is captured by the sweetness of grace, can not do that to which it is snatched, because it retains the true power of not acting, even under snatching grace: although it cannot be that the not-acting itself, be coupled with the operation of grace in the same will at the same time. Which in the following chapter he embraces in fewer words, For the power, he says, of dissenting is not repugnant to the actual motion of grace and to consent; although it cannot be that actual dissent, be joined with the actual motion of God.
pass_b: Thesis XLIV. He repeats and presses the same point in chapter 20 of the same book: 'We say that free choice, however strongly and effectively it has been anticipated and determined to do good by the delight of grace, can still not only fail to do the good but even do evil. This is true not in the composite sense, as the common phrase has it, but in the divided sense.

'At the very time when the will's choice is placed under the delight of grace that moves it effectively, and even while it is performing the good act of will, there is in that same will the power not to perform it, and even to sin. This is not because ceasing from the act it is then eliciting, or an actual sin, could coexist with the influence of delighting grace (which the composite sense would require), but because the power to cease and to sin can be joined with that same grace at the same time in the same choice of the will.

'Two contrary acts are opposed and cannot be in the same will at once; but powers for opposites are not opposed, either to one another or to the opposite acts, and they dwell together in the same subject at the same time, whether it is acting or at rest. So the will, however much it is captivated by the sweetness of grace, can refrain from doing what it is drawn to, since it keeps a real power of not acting even under the grace that draws it, although not acting itself cannot be combined with the working of grace in the same will at the same time.'

In the next chapter he puts it more briefly: 'The power of dissenting does not conflict with the actual motion of grace and with consent, although actual dissent cannot be joined with God's actual motion.'

sections.title: Jansenius's preferred concord: freedom as acting from one's own reason
sections.pass_a: XLV. But although Jansenius, and those who are in the same opinion with him, acknowledge that with the efficacy of divine grace is so to be reconciled the indifference, or that power, to good and to evil, to acting and not acting, which they do not deny is found in all those who live in this mortal body; and in which many seem to place the very essence of liberty: nevertheless they maintain that the true and genuine concord of divine grace with free will is not to be sought thence. Since Augustine and his first disciples establish that concord otherwise. Namely that they may reconcile grace with free choice, they simply say, that it does not therefore take away free choice, because it makes that free choice is not idle like a stone and does nothing, nor that unwilling it is forced to good, but that it itself also wills and acts, for they defined free as that which is in our power: but they said that that is in our power which is done when we will, or which someone if he wills does, if he does not will does not do. Which being posited it follows that absolutely every will, or rational volition is free: because just as it is impossible, that it not be done when we will, and be done when we do not will, so consequently it is impossible, that it be not in our power, and by this very thing not be free. And therefore since grace performs nothing else than that we elicit a good volition, from the right judgment of reason, by this very thing it makes that we act freely, nor does it destroy our liberty but establishes it. Which way of reconciling human liberty with the infallible efficacy of divine grace, Jansenius judges to be the best of all and most genuine on the Grace of Christ the Saviour book 8. chap. 19. And that because, according to him, the essence of liberty considered in general, by no means consists in indifference, by which someone can will or not will, will this, or the contrary: but rather in this that someone is moved to willing and acting, not by some external force, nor by brute necessity, but by the judgment of his own reason, and to that extent is Lord of his act.
pass_b: Thesis XLV. Jansenius and those who share his view do acknowledge that the efficacy of divine grace must be reconciled in this way with indifference, that is, with the power toward good and evil, toward acting and not acting, which they do not deny is found in all who live in this mortal body, and in which many seem to place the very essence of freedom. Even so, they insist that the true and genuine harmony of divine grace with free will is not to be sought there, because Augustine and his first disciples set out that harmony differently.

To reconcile grace with free choice, they say simply that grace does not take away free choice, since it causes free choice not to lie idle like a stone and do nothing, nor to be forced to the good against its will, but itself to will and act. For they defined as free what is in our power, and they said that what is in our power is what happens when we will it, or what someone does if he wills and does not do if he does not will. On these premises it follows that every act of will whatever, that is, every rational volition, is free. Just as it is impossible for it not to happen when we will it and to happen when we do not, so it is impossible for it not to be in our power and thereby not free.

Since grace, then, does nothing but cause us to elicit a good volition from the right judgment of reason, by that very fact it causes us to act freely, and so it does not destroy our freedom but establishes it. Jansenius judges this way of reconciling human freedom with the infallible efficacy of divine grace to be the best and most genuine of all (De gratia Christi Salvatoris, book 8, chapter 19). For on his view the essence of freedom considered in general does not consist at all in the indifference by which one can will or not will, will this or its contrary, but rather in being moved to will and act not by some external force or brute necessity but by the judgment of one's own reason, and so far being master of one's own act.

sections.title: Same working, different essence: Jansenius and the Thomists part
sections.pass_a: XLVI. However although Jansenius and the recent Thomists agree in this that the grace of Christ, through which men are converted and work well, is grace efficacious by itself, which subjects free choice to itself, but is in no way subject to free choice; and which, that its effect may follow, does not wait for the consent of the human will, but effects that consent infallibly and powerfully: yet they disagree among themselves about the nature and substance of that grace: nor do they explain in the same way in what thing it consists and is placed. To both the mode of operating of that grace is the same, but its essence diverse.
pass_b: Thesis XLVI. Jansenius and the recent Thomists agree that the grace of Christ by which people are converted and do good is grace efficacious of itself, which brings free choice under itself and is in no way subject to it, and which does not wait for the human will's consent for its effect to follow but brings that consent about infallibly and powerfully.

Yet they disagree about the nature and substance of that grace, and do not explain in the same way what it consists in and where it lies. For both, the way this grace works is the same; what it is differs.

lemmas.latin: de gratiae illius natura atque substantia
lemmas.gloss: about the nature and substance of that grace
the mode of operating is the same
but its essence diverse

choices.why: Kept as in I-XXX: grace whose efficacy comes from the grace itself, not from the consent that follows.

sections.title: Agreed: an immediate motion of the will, not an abiding habit
sections.pass_a: XLVII. It is agreed indeed between both that that grace, without which no one is converted to God and acts well, and which all who receive, certainly and infallibly are converted and act well, is a certain help which moves and affects the will itself by itself and immediately, not however the intellect alone; nor is it to be placed in any permanent habit. But what it is, is not altogether agreed between these and those: nay not even among the Thomists themselves.
pass_b: Thesis XLVII. Both sides agree that the grace without which no one turns to God and does good, and whose recipients are all surely and infallibly converted and do good, is an aid that moves and affects the will itself, of itself and immediately, and not the intellect alone; and that it is not to be located in any abiding habit.
But what it is, the two sides do not fully agree; indeed, not even the Thomists agree among themselves.

lemmas.latin: per se & immediate movet atque afficit
lemmas.gloss: moves and affects by itself and immediately

lemmas.latin: nec eam in ullo habitu permanenti constituendam esse
lemmas.gloss: nor is it to be placed in any permanent habit
nay not even among the Thomists themselves

choices.why: Habitual (abiding) versus actual (passing) grace, as in the earlier grace loci.

sections.title: Three Thomist accounts of the premotion; Alvarez's 'virtual motion'
sections.pass_a: XLVIII. For although all those signify that efficacious help by the name of physical predetermination, and say that it is a gratuitous and prior motion of God, which moves and applies the created will to working well; there are nevertheless some who say that that premotion of God by which human wills are moved to acting well, holds itself after the mode of a quality not permanent, but transient with the operation of the will itself. But others say that the actual motion by which God moves and applies the will to operating, is really the very operation of the will, in so far as it proceeds from God, applying and premoving the will to acting efficaciously. Finally others maintain that that prior motion, neither holds itself after the mode of a quality received in the will, nor is the same with the very operation of the will; but something which has a certain incomplete being, in the way in which colours are in the air, and the virtue of the art in the instrument of the artificer, which by a proper and fitting name can be called virtual motion. As is to be seen in Didacus Alvarez book 3. on the Helps of divine grace disput. 19. where he defends this last opinion as true and his own.
pass_b: Thesis XLVIII. All of them call this efficacious aid by the name of physical predetermination, and say that it is a gratuitous and prior motion of God that moves the created will and applies it to doing good. Yet some say that this premotion of God, by which human wills are moved to do good, is in the manner of a quality that does not remain but passes away with the will's own operation.

Others say that the actual motion by which God moves the will and applies it to act is really the will's operation itself, insofar as it comes from God, who applies the will to act and efficaciously premoves it.

Finally, others hold that this prior motion is neither in the manner of a quality received in the will nor the same as the will's operation, but something with a kind of incomplete being, as colours are in the air and the power of the craft is in the craftsman's tool, which may properly and fittingly be called a 'virtual motion'. So Diego Alvarez, De auxiliis divinae gratiae, book 3, disputation 19, who defends this last opinion as true and as his own.

lemmas.gloss: by the name of physical predetermination

lemmas.latin: ad modum qualitatis non permanentis, sed transeuntis
lemmas.gloss: after the mode of a quality not permanent, but transient

lemmas.latin: per modum quo colores sunt in aere
lemmas.gloss: in the way in which colours are in the air
virtual motion

choices.why: Alvarez's term: an incomplete, passing being like the craftsman's power in his tool; 'virtuous' would mislead.

bible_refs: Diego Alvarez OP, De auxiliis divinae gratiae et humani arbitrii viribus (Rome, 1610), book 3, disputations 18-19.

sections.title: Alvarez: the will is passive to the premotion, active in its act
sections.pass_a: XLIX. Thence however he gathers that that help of God, prior to the action of the created will, is produced in it effectively by God alone, and in no way depends efficiently on the influx of the will itself: and so that the will in order to that prior help of God holds itself passively: although the same will holds itself actively and freely, in order to the free act, to which it is moved by that prior help. Of the disputation just cited number sixth.
pass_b: Thesis XLIX. From this he infers that this aid of God, which precedes the created will's action, is produced in the will effectively by God alone and in no way depends efficiently on any influence of the will itself. So with respect to that prior aid of God the will is passive, although the same will is active and free with respect to the free act to which that prior aid moves it. The disputation just cited, section 6.

lemmas.gloss: by God alone
holds itself passively
holds itself actively and freely

choices.english: is passive ... is active (literal pass: holds itself passively/actively)
choices.why: The scholastic 'se habere' idiom rendered by the plain verb.

sections.title: Not in our power, yet we can hinder it: Alvarez's man commanded to fly
sections.pass_a: L. Further those Doctors acknowledge that that motion of God prior and necessary for every good work is not in the power of man; because it is given and denied from the divine good pleasure. But nevertheless they affirm that it is in the faculty of our will to hinder itself so that it not have that motion. Whence they gather that, if he does not work the act, which is in the precept, it will be imputed to him for fault, because by his fault he hindered himself, so that the efficacious help was not given him, which was necessary, that he might actually work the act of virtue, which is in the precept: as if God imposed on a man the precept of flying, and as much as is on his part, offered him wings, and the help necessary that he might fly; but he by his liberty should answer; Lord I neither will to receive wings nor to fly; deservedly he would be reputed guilty, and a transgressor of the precept, even if he could not fly without wings, because by his fault he hindered himself, so that they were not given him by God. Which are the words of the same Alvarez in the book just now cited disputation eighteenth num. 20. Where he confirms his doctrine by the saying of Augustine, That men are not helped by the grace of God, the cause is in themselves, not in God.
pass_b: Thesis L. These doctors also acknowledge that this motion of God, prior to and necessary for every good work, is not in a person's power, since it is given and withheld at God's good pleasure. Yet they maintain that our will has the capacity to prevent itself from receiving that motion.

From this they infer: 'If a person does not perform the act that is commanded, it will be counted against him as a fault, because by his own fault he prevented the efficacious aid from being given him, which he needed in order actually to perform the act of virtue that is commanded. It is as if God laid on someone a command to fly and, as far as lay with God, offered him wings and the help he needed to fly, and the man answered in his freedom, "Lord, I do not want to take wings or to fly": he would rightly be held guilty and a breaker of the command, even though he could not fly without wings, because by his own fault he prevented their being given him by God.'

These are the words of the same Alvarez in the book just cited, disputation 18, section 20, where he supports his teaching with Augustine's saying: 'That people are not helped by God's grace, the cause lies in themselves, not in God.'

lemmas.gloss: to hinder itself so that it not have that motion

sections.title: Why premotion is needed: dependence on the First Cause, not only the fall
sections.pass_a: LI. However the necessity of that help efficaciously premoving and predetermining the will to every pious operation they do not derive simply from the corruption and infirmity of the human will; but in general from the dependence of every second cause on the First, without whose impulse and prior motion, there is no cause which can do anything, according to their hypotheses. And besides from the indifference of the free will, which is not apt to do anything, unless it be determined by a superior agent.
pass_b: Thesis LI. These doctors do not derive the need for this aid, which effectively premoves and predetermines the will to every devout action, simply from the corruption and weakness of the human will. They derive it in general from the dependence of every secondary cause on the First Cause, without whose impulse and prior motion, on their assumptions, no cause can do anything at all; and further from the indifference of the free will, which is not fit to do anything unless a higher agent determines it.

lemmas.latin: non arcessunt simpliciter ex voluntatis humanae corruptione
lemmas.gloss: they do not derive simply from the corruption of the human will

lemmas.latin: ex dependentia omnis causae secundae a Prima
lemmas.gloss: from the dependence of every second cause on the First
unless it be determined by a superior agent

choices.why: Thomist physical premotion and predetermination (Banez, Alvarez); kept as in XXX.

sections.title: Physical premotion presupposes a moral motion through the object
sections.pass_a: LII. But although they place that efficacious help in a certain motion physically predetermining the will; they acknowledge however that it presupposes a moral motion, which is done through a congruous proposal of the object, through which that object appears lovable and fitting to the will. For neither can the will desire anything, unless first through the intellect it be proposed to it as fitting. And therefore that no one through the help of grace is physically determined to pursuing good, without his mind having been illuminated by knowledge of that good, and the will invited to desiring it, and morally inclined by internal suasions and suggestions of the holy spirit. But from that never follows, according to their doctrine, the consent of the will, unless that other help be added, which moves the will to that consent efficaciously and physically.
pass_b: Thesis LII. Although they place this efficacious aid in a motion that physically predetermines the will, they acknowledge that it presupposes a moral motion, brought about by a fitting presentation of the object through which that object appears lovable and suited to the will. For the will cannot desire anything unless the intellect first presents it to the will as suited to it.

So no one is physically determined by the aid of grace to pursue the good unless his mind has been enlightened with knowledge of that good, and his will invited to desire it and morally inclined by the inward persuasions and promptings of the Holy Spirit. Yet on their teaching the will's consent never follows from this unless that other aid is added which moves the will effectively and physically to consent.

lemmas.gloss: presupposes a moral motion
through a congruous proposal of the object
by internal suasions and suggestions of the holy spirit

choices.why: Scholastic contrast: a physical motion works on the faculty itself; a moral motion works by attracting and persuading through the object (as XLII and LII explain).
